ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: On the left side of the figure, two molecules of acetic acid are drawn approaching each other; each molecule has a carboxylic acid structure: one carbonyl oxygen and one O-H group; the two molecules are arranged so that the O-H hydrogen of one molecule points toward the carbonyl oxygen of the other molecule, forming mutually corresponding interactions. On the right side of the figure, two molecules of acetyl chloride are drawn, with a carbonyl oxygen in the structure, but the original O-H position in the carboxylic acid is replaced by an O-Cl/chlorine-related group, with no O-H hydrogen that can serve as a hydrogen-bond donor. Reasoning: The question compares the ability to form dimers in the gas phase. An acetic acid molecule has both an O-H hydrogen-bond donor and a carbonyl oxygen hydrogen-bond acceptor, so two acetic acid molecules can combine stably into a dimer through strong, mutual hydrogen bonds. Acetyl chloride lacks an O-H hydrogen-bond donor and cannot form the same strong complementary hydrogen bonds, and can only mainly rely on weaker dipole-dipole attractions and other polar interactions. Therefore acetic acid forms dimers more easily than acetyl chloride.
